title: Building a RAG Pipeline from Scratch
excerpt: What I learned wiring up chunking, embeddings, a vector store and an LLM by hand — before reaching for a framework.
content:
## Why build it from scratch first

Before leaning on LangChain or LlamaIndex, I built a minimal RAG pipeline by hand: a chunker, a Sentence-Transformers embedder, a tiny in-memory vector index, and a prompt that stitched retrieved chunks into a Mistral call. It took a weekend and completely changed how I read framework code afterwards.

## The four moving parts

1. **Chunking.** Fixed-size windows are the wrong default. Overlap + sentence-aware splitting fixed 80% of my hallucinations.
2. **Embeddings.** `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` is a shockingly good baseline. Don't reach for OpenAI embeddings until you have proof they beat it on *your* data.
3. **Retrieval.** Cosine similarity is fine — but reranking the top-20 with a cross-encoder beat every clever prompt trick I tried.
4. **Prompt.** Grounding the answer in cited chunks (`[1]`, `[2]`) made evaluation dramatically easier, because I could see where the model was pulling from.

## Where LangChain earned its keep

Once I ported it to LangChain LCEL, the *chain* got shorter but the *observability* got a lot better. Retrievers, prompts and models become composable primitives you can swap without touching glue code. Would still recommend building it raw first.

title: What I Learned Fine-Tuning BERT
excerpt: Class imbalance, learning-rate warmup, and the moment the model stopped predicting only the majority class.
content:
## The task

Multi-class sentiment classification on a customer review dataset with a nasty 70/20/10 class split. First run: 71% accuracy, F1 on the minority class close to zero. Classic.

## The three things that actually moved the needle

1. **Class-weighted loss.** Passing per-class weights into `CrossEntropyLoss` was a bigger unlock than any architectural tweak.
2. **LR warmup + linear decay.** BERT hates high LR from step 0. A 10% warmup schedule stabilized training immediately.
3. **Actually looking at the confusion matrix.** Accuracy was hiding the story. Once I plotted per-class precision / recall I could see exactly which pairs the model was confusing (spoiler: neutral vs. slightly-positive).

## Takeaway

Fine-tuning is 20% model, 80% data + evaluation discipline. Precision, recall and F1 per class are non-negotiable on imbalanced data.

title: Notes on Agentic AI: Tools, Memory, and Loops
excerpt: Why the interesting research isn't the model — it's the scaffolding around it.
content:
## The shift

A chatbot answers a question. An agent decides what to do next. That gap is where almost all the interesting engineering lives right now: tool use, memory, planning loops, self-critique.

## What I keep coming back to

- **Tool interfaces matter more than model choice.** A well-typed tool with a crisp docstring beats a bigger model with a vague API.
- **Short memory > long memory.** Aggressive summarization of the scratchpad keeps agents on-task longer than dumping the whole history.
- **Loops need brakes.** A max-steps counter and a self-critique step have saved me from a lot of runaway token bills.

Still early days — but building even a small agent teaches you more about LLM behavior than a month of reading papers.
